newsitem.title: UK: N. Ireland peace process seen in serious danger.
newsitem.headline: N. Ireland peace process seen in serious danger.

text.p: Northern Ireland's two-year peace process appeared to be unravelling on Tuesday after a twin attack from the Protestant majority's underground Loyalist militia and political leadership.

Spokesmen for more than 400 Loyalist activists jailed for security offences over the past two decades declared a vote of no confidence in the process in a move which could threaten a two-year ceasefire by Loyalist gunmen still at large.

At the same time David Trimble, the head of the mainstream pro-British Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), accused the London government of caving in to IRA Irish nationalist guerrillas and said three-month-old peace talks were in serious jeopardy.
Irish officials were downcast at the news and said the outlook for the talks, already hamstrung by the absence of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, was very bleak.
The air of crisis was heightened by the discovery in Belfast on Sunday night of a 250-pound (120-kg) car bomb planted by a breakaway Irish republican guerrilla group.
It followed a police raid in London last week on an IRA (Irish Republican Army) bomb factory where devices were being prepared for a new attack in the campaign to end British rule of the province.
Four men appeared in court in London on Monday charged with plotting bomb attacks following the raid, in which one suspect was shot dead.

John White, a leader of the Ulster Democratic Party, which is close to one wing of the Loyalist underground militia, said jailed Loyalists felt they had got nothing in return for a two-year ceasefire and disavowed the peace process.
They were angry at the surge in violence by the IRA, which ended a 17-month ceasefire in February, and felt there was no point in maintaining their own ceasefire.
"They felt that Republicans are purely talking of peace while preparing for war," said White.

Sources close to the Loyalists said they expected Britain to free a substantial number of prisoners as a goodwill gesture for maintaining the truce. But Britain says there will be no amnesties for anyone convicted of security offences.
Trimble told a news conference that the British and Irish governments were preparing to bend the rules to allow Sinn Fein to take part in the talks and accused London of betrayal.

He said the British and Irish sponsors of the talks were preparing to ease conditions under which guerrillas would disarm to try to persuade the IRA to call a truce and earn Sinn Fein a seat at the talks.

Britain and Ireland say only a new ceasefire will allow Sinn Fein to join the talks. But the IRA says it will not negotiate the surrender of its guerrilla arsenals until a new political settlement is achieved.

"Back in February (British Prime Minister) John Major said the talks would go forward with or without Sinn Fein. Now is he prepared to do that or is he still carrying a torch for Sinn Fein?" Trimble said.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said last month that a new IRA ceasefire was a real possibility but the wave of optimism crashed days later when British police found 10 tonnes of explosive and weapons in a major IRA arms haul.

The talks, which started in June, group every major political organisation in Northern Ireland except Sinn Fein, the politcal wing of the IRA, whose war against British rule lies at the heart of the 25-year conflict.
